title: Plum's Midnight Ride
markdown:
Plum was a Pony Express foal, which meant messages, important ones, zipped all over the countryside. His stable smelled of warm hay and sleepy snores. He loved the idea of the job: galloping with the wind in his mane, a speedy delivery hero, brown fur and flying hooves, tales and tidings faster than a firefly’s flash. Off I go, he would whisper in daylight, practising to the water trough, to the gate, to the square of sun on the floor.

But—and this was a big wiggly but—Plum had a secret that made his hooves tap-tap-tap the floor. He was afraid of the dark. Really, hide-under-the-hay afraid. Shadows stretched like wobbly giants. Rustles seemed to whisper. His tummy did flip-flops like a troupe of acrobatic mice. He squeezed his eyes shut and wished the sun would stay up forever.

One sunny afternoon a very important message arrived, paper as soft as a dandelion puff, ribbon the colour of a blueberry, for Farmer McGregor across Farmer Giles’s fields and past the shadowy Whispering Woods. Not just any message. An invitation to the most wonderful MIDNIGHT FEAST: carrot cakes piled high, apple tarts with sugary dew, maybe berry juice. Plum’s tail gave a hopeful wiggle. He had to deliver it. His chance to be a real hero.

The sun was already dipping, fiery orange and soft lavender. The message needed to arrive before midnight, or Farmer Giles’s prize pumpkins would be munched by snackers before anyone knew there was a feast. A knot of worry tightened in Plum’s chest. He knew what he had to do, even if his knees felt like jelly.

Off I go, he told himself, and with a deep breath that puffed his chest almost grown-up size, he nudged the invitation into his saddlebag. “Right then.” A tiny hopeful trot, surprisingly steady, carried him out of the cozy stable into the great wide growing-dark world.

First he trotted through Farmer Giles’s fields. Tickly grass. Golden butterscotch light. Happy little thuds. Crickets winding their tiny clocks. A sigh of breeze that smelled of warm earth and almost-ripe pumpkins. “This isn’t so bad,” Plum murmured, and believed it for a whole field. He even practised a small gallop, invitation bumping like a friendly heart. Off I go, off I go, the words matching his hooves until the gold began to thin.

At the edge of the Whispering Woods the gold faded. Trees loomed, reaching branches. Wind went through the leaves like whispers that tickled his ears. Rustle. Scrabble. A shadow-thing with extra-long claws? Plum froze, hooves glued like toffee. He wanted to whinny for Mum, for a friendly squirrel, for the square of sun on the stable floor. Oh dear, a squeak. The invitation suddenly felt heavier than paper.

A small quick voice, bright as a daisy. “Lost, little foal? Or admiring the dew-covered moss?” Wick the weasel popped from behind a mossy log, nose twitching. Quick, clever, a nose that could sniff a runaway berry from a mile. He saw Plum trembling. “Whoa there. It’s the wind playing tag with the leaves, and sleepy beetles having a nighttime wiggle. Not a monster. I know a shortcut. Much faster if you stick with me. Out before you can say midnight snack.”

Plum hesitated. The dark felt like a heavy blanket. His brave feeling tried to sneak away under the hay he was not even standing on. Wick’s grin was friendly, eyes sparking mischief and kindness, the sort of spark that makes a shortcut seem like a song.

“Okay,” Plum whispered, shaky as jelly on a wobbly plate. “But it’s very dark in there.”

“That’s why I’m here. I can see in the dark. Eyes like little nighttime lanterns. Listen.” Wick made a funny huffing sound, a tiny sleepy dragon. “That’s just Cerys Burrow waking up for a stretch and a sniff. Grumpy before a second cup of chamomile.”

Plum listened. It did sound like a grumpy yawn, not a monster. Wick led, quick paws barely sounding, cool damp air in Plum’s nostrils. They passed a beetle who really was having a nighttime wiggle, and a puddle that held a piece of moon like a dropped coin. Plum followed, trying to ignore shadowy sprites at the edge of vision, focusing on Wick’s sure movements and cheerful chatter, a little song in the dark. Off I go, off I go, the words matching his hooves.

They emerged blinking in silvery moon-rise. Plum’s heart did a happy flip. Ahead, Farmer McGregor’s lights twinkled like fallen stars. The woods were behind him. The invitation was still in the bag. “Thank you, Wick. You were like a tiny helpful lighthouse.”

“Any time.” Wick winked, pointing to a gnarled ancient tree that stood alone between woods and farm. “Watch the Old Willow. Looks grumpy. Just old and sleepy, like a very old teddy bear.”

Plum’s tummy lurched. The biggest most imposing tree in the countryside: branches like bony fingers, roots like grasping claws. He had to get past it before midnight. He could almost taste carrot cake. The dark around the Willow seemed extra deep, extra still, extra hushed. A shiver. His brave feeling hid like a shy mouse. Turn back, little foal. Wick had already slipped back toward the moss, as weasels do when a job is done. This last bit was Plum’s.

He paused, panic tightening his throat. Rough bark if he got too close. Earthy smell from deep roots, older than any feast. Then he thought of the pumpkin snackers, the farmers’ smiles, Wick who was not afraid and had been kind, Cerys Burrow and her chamomile, the beetle’s wiggle, the puddle’s moon. Another breath, a little stronger. One hesitant step. Another. Wind sighed through ancient branches, creaky, heart pounding. He squeezed his eyes shut, pictured the invitation, the blueberry ribbon, the happy faces. Opened them. Galloped. Past grasping roots, bony branches, hushed stillness. He did not look back. He just went. Hooves a rhythm of courage. Off I go.

He was past it. The Old Willow was just a tree. Very old, very big, just a tree. The dark was not so bad when you were moving, moonlight on your back. A fizzy feeling, sunshine and bravery mixed. He raced for the farm, invitation bumping gently. The clock tower chimed eleven. He’d made it.

Farmer McGregor came out with a lantern and a crinkly smile and patted Plum’s flank. “Well done, young fella. Just in time.” He took the blueberry ribbon as if it were a prize. From the kitchen drifted carrot cake and apple tart.

Trotting home, the moon seemed to smile, a silvery hug. Shadows were quiet friendly shapes. Rustling was night business, ants and mice and, far off, one more yawn from Cerys Burrow. He had delivered the invitation. He had not hidden under the hay. The Willow, looking back, only looked sleepy, a teddy bear of a tree keeping the lane.

In his stable, first hint of dawn in soft pinks, Plum curled in familiar hay. Tired, warm, happy, as if he had swallowed a little sunshine. His hooves might still wobble sometimes. He could still be brave. A fluffy owl blinked from a branch. Plum did not flinch. He nodded, a soft nicker, a greeting to a fellow night-dweller, then rested. Off I go, he thought toward whatever message came next, no matter when it arrived, even if the sun had already gone.
